summary: German has eight subject pronouns – ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie – plus the polite Sie. A subject pronoun is never left out, because the verb ending alone is not enough (Ich bin …, not *Bin …). er, sie and es follow the grammatical gender of the noun, not the real sex: der Tisch → er, die Lampe → sie, das Mädchen → es. Three words look alike: sie (she, verb in -t), sie (they, verb in -en) and Sie (you, polite, capital S, verb in -en).

askYourself: Who is the subject: me (ich), the person I talk to, or someone/something else?
Am I talking to one person or several – and do I say du or Sie to them?
Is it a thing? Then what is the gender of its noun: der → er, die → sie, das → es?
One or several? Several people or things are always sie, with the verb in -en (sie sind).
Polite Sie: did I write the capital S and use the “they” form of the verb?
steps: Choose the pronoun by person, number, gender of the noun and du/Sie.
Give the verb the matching ending.

traps: Never drop the pronoun: Ich bin müde, not *Bin müde (in Greek είμαι alone is enough).
ich is lower-case inside a sentence – unlike English I.
A girl is es in grammar (das Mädchen … es), though people often say sie once they know her name.
Sie (polite) takes the verb of “they”: Sie sind, never *Sie bist / *Sie ist.
ihr (you, plural) is also ihr = (to) her and ihr = her/their (possessive); the verb shows which: ihr seid.

quiz.why: der-nouns are er, even for things.
Every plural is sie, whatever the gender.

quiz.q: You talk to your new boss. “You” is …
You talk to two friends at once. “You” is …
quiz.why: Several people you each say du to: ihr.

quiz.q: Which form goes with polite Sie?
quiz.why: Sie takes the verb form of “they”.

seeAlso.note: Arabic splits “you” and “they” by gender (anta / anti, hum / hunna) and has a dual (antumā, humā); the pronoun is often dropped because the verb shows the person.
Hebrew also splits “you” and “they” by gender (atá / at, atem / aten, hem / hen); in the past tense ani / ata can be left out, in the present not.
Chinese has one spoken tā for he / she / it (他 / 她 / 它 differ only in writing), plural with 们 (我们, 你们, 他们) and a polite 您 – no endings, no cases.
The pronoun chooses the form of sein: ich bin, du bist, er ist …
